#10899. CORS Error Fix: Diagnose Console Errors and Configure Headers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every frontend developer will eventually stare at a CORS error in the browser console, watching an API call fail for reasons that seem opaque. A CORS error fix requires understanding what the browser is actually telling you, matching that specific message to its root cause, and applying a targeted, security-conscious server configuration.

The scheme, host, and port together define an "origin." https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins (different schemes), as are https://example.com and https://api.example.com (different hosts). https://example.com and https://example.com:443 are the same origin because port 443 is the default for HTTPS, and browsers omit it in origin comparisons. The browser enforces the same-origin policy on client-side JavaScript reading responses, not on sending requests. This distinction trips up many developers: the server may still receive and fully process the request; the browser simply refuses to expose the response to the calling code. The request lands, the database row gets written, and the browser throws an error anyway. The policy exists to prevent a malicious page from silently reading sensitive data from another origin using the user's ambient credentials.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a controlled opt-in mechanism via HTTP response headers. The server signals to the browser that a specific foreign origin is permitted to read its responses. Four headers control the mechanism: Access-Control-Allow-Origin specifies which origin is allowed, and Access-Control-Allow-Methods declares which HTTP methods are permitted. Access-Control-Allow-Headers lists which custom or non-simple headers the client may send, while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials indicates whether the browser should expose the response to credentialed requests.

The browser does not treat all cross-origin requests equally. "Simple" requests use GET, HEAD, or POST with a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain, and no custom headers. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not a simple request and triggers a preflight.

Simple requests go directly to the server, and the browser evaluates the CORS headers on the response. Anything else triggers a preflight request: an OPTIONS call the browser sends automatically before the actual request, asking the server whether the real request would be acceptable. If the OPTIONS response lacks the proper CORS headers, the browser never sends the real request at all.

A typical Chrome DevTools error reads: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Two origins appear in this message. The URL after "fetch at" is the target server, the resource the code tried to reach. The value after "from origin" is the page's own origin, the one making the request. Chrome is stating that the target server's response did not include an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that matches the requesting origin, so the browser blocked the response from reaching JavaScript.

The most common variant is the missing header: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The server simply did not include the header at all.

When the console says Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check, the server either did not respond to the OPTIONS request correctly or returned a non-2xx status code for it.

Redirect variant: Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request. Developers commonly misdiagnose this one. It occurs when the URL triggers a redirect before reaching the application handler. Typical culprits include HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrades, trailing-slash normalization (e.g., /api/data redirecting to /api/data/), or a load balancer rewriting URLs. The browser's preflight OPTIONS request follows the redirect, and the Fetch specification (§4.8) forbids following redirects on preflight requests, so the entire flow fails. Fix the URL so no redirect occurs.

Credential variant: The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. When fetch is called with credentials: 'include' or XMLHttpRequest sets withCredentials = true, the server must respond with the exact requesting origin, not *. The browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials.

Entry point: What does the console error say?

Each branch leads to a specific fix section in this article. Bookmark this decision tree and start here every time a CORS error surfaces.

Before modifying any server code, verify what the server actually returns by simulating a preflight request from the command line:

The -i flag prints response headers. -X OPTIONS sets the HTTP method to OPTIONS, mimicking the browser's preflight. The Origin header declares the requesting origin. Access-Control-Request-Method tells the server which method the real request would use. Access-Control-Request-Headers lists the custom headers the real request would include.

If these are absent, the server is not configured for CORS. If the response is a 301 or 302 redirect, the redirect variant is the culprit.

During local development, the least-configuration way to eliminate cross-origin issues is to proxy API requests through the dev server so the browser sees all traffic as same-origin.

With this configuration, a fetch('/api/users') call from the frontend at http://localhost:5173 is forwarded to http://localhost:3001/users. The browser never sees a cross-origin request. Without changeOrigin: true, the Host header sent upstream retains the dev server's hostname, which may cause backend rejections if the target validates the Host header. This is strictly a development-only solution. Production builds served from a static host will not have this proxy, so proper server-side CORS headers remain necessary.

Tested with: cors@2.8.5, express@4.18, Node.js 20 LTS. The cors package API surface has been stable since 2.x; check the changelog if you are on an earlier major version.

The simplest fix to unblock development uses the cors npm package with its defaults:

This applies Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every response. It unblocks any requesting origin, but it cannot be used with credentialed requests, and it exposes every endpoint to every origin on the internet. Any page an attacker controls can issue authenticated requests to your API and read the responses if the user is logged in. Move past it quickly.

For production, validate the incoming Origin header against an allowlist and reflect only permitted origins:

The origin function receives the Origin header value and calls callback(null, true) to allow the request. When true is passed, the cors package automatically reflects the incoming Origin header in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Vary: Origin. This satisfies the credential requirement and prevents open CORS misconfiguration. Setting credentials: true in the options causes the middleware to include the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true response header. The cors middleware automatically handles OPTIONS preflight responses when applied at the app level.

Tested with: Next.js 14.x App Router, Node.js 20 LTS. The OPTIONS handler behavior and middleware matcher syntax changed between Next.js 13 and 15; exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach.

The cors npm package does not plug directly into the Next.js App Router (as of Next.js 13+). Instead, set headers manually in a route handler:

The OPTIONS export explicitly handles preflight requests and returns a 204 No Content with the required CORS headers. Without this, Next.js returns a 405 Method Not Allowed for OPTIONS in some versions (the exact behavior changed between 13 and 14), triggering the preflight failure variant. Exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach. The getCorsHeaders function returns an empty object for disallowed or absent origins, ensuring that server capabilities (supported methods and headers) are not disclosed to untrusted origins.

For projects with many API routes, centralizing CORS logic in middleware avoids repetition:

The matcher restricts this middleware to API routes only. Access-Control-Max-Age instructs browsers to cache preflight results. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400. The Vary: Origin header is only set when a cross-origin request is detected (the Origin header is present and allowed), avoiding unnecessary CDN cache fragmentation on same-origin or server-to-server requests. CORS headers including Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers are only sent to allowed origins, preventing server capability disclosure to untrusted origins.

Tested with: Nginx 1.24+. The map directive behavior is stable across modern Nginx versions.

When Nginx sits in front of a backend, it is often the right place to manage CORS centrally. Important: Do not use if with add_header inside a location block -- Nginx's if block causes all parent-scope add_header directives to be silently ignored, breaking CORS headers on actual (non-OPTIONS) API responses.

The map directive builds an allowlist: if $http_origin matches a listed value, $cors_origin is set to that value; otherwise it remains empty. The always parameter ensures headers are added even on error responses (4xx, 5xx), which is critical because Nginx's add_header without always silently drops headers on non-2xx responses.

Nginx's if directive creates a new configuration context. Any add_header inside an if block discards all add_header directives from the enclosing scope.

Why the if block contains all headers and return 204: By placing return 204 inside the if block, the OPTIONS request is fully handled there and never reaches the outer add_header directives or proxy_pass. Non-OPTIONS requests skip the if block entirely and the outer scope's add_header directives and proxy_pass handle them. This separation avoids the inheritance pitfall: each request path (OPTIONS vs. non-OPTIONS) has its own complete, self-contained set of headers.

Note on empty $cors_origin: When the allowlist excludes the origin, $cors_origin resolves to an empty string, and Nginx emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: (a blank header). Browsers will reject CORS for the request, which is the correct security outcome. However, emitting a blank header is technically non-conformant with RFC 6454. The most robust production solution is to handle CORS in the application layer (Express/Next.js) and have Nginx proxy transparently, or to use OpenResty/Lua for conditional header suppression.

After deploying, verify that both curl -X OPTIONS and curl -X GET against the same URL return the expected CORS headers.

A frequent source of the redirect CORS variant is a proxy_pass trailing-slash mismatch. If the location block is location /api but proxy_pass is http://127.0.0.1:3001 (no trailing slash), Nginx may issue a redirect for /api/ normalization before the request reaches the handler. Similarly, a return 301 https://... rule placed before the CORS location block can redirect the OPTIONS preflight. The fix is straightforward: ensure trailing slashes match between location and proxy_pass, and place any redirect rules after or outside the API location block so they do not intercept OPTIONS requests.

Use an explicit origin allowlist. Avoid * when credentials are involved; the browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials: 'include'.

Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Methods to only the methods the API actually uses. Listing every HTTP method widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

Set Access-Control-Max-Age to cache preflight responses. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400 (24 hours). Use 7200 as a safe cross-browser default, or 86400 if your users are primarily on Firefox and you want fewer preflight round-trips.

Include Vary: Origin on every response where Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set conditionally. Without it, CDN or proxy caches may serve a CORS response cached for one origin to a different origin, causing intermittent failures.

Never mirror the request Origin header back without validating it against an allowlist. This is an open CORS misconfiguration that effectively disables the same-origin policy for any attacker-controlled origin.

Do not install browser extensions that disable CORS either -- they mask the problem during development and expose you to real cross-origin attacks on every other site you visit.

Avoid adding CORS headers in both the application framework and Nginx simultaneously. Duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers cause the browser's CORS origin comparison to fail; the browser receives the response but blocks JavaScript from reading it, producing the same CORS error the fix was meant to resolve.

Read the console error, match it against the decision tree, apply the targeted fix, and verify with the curl preflight command. Use the decision tree above as a reference for every future CORS error.

#10897. Deploying Speech-to-Speech on Hugging Face

Speech-to-Speech (S2S) is an exciting new project from Hugging Face that combines several advanced models to create a seamless, almost magical experience: you speak, and the system responds with a synthesized voice.

The project implements a cascaded pipeline leveraging models available through the Transformers library on the Hugging Face hub. The pipeline consists of the following components:

What's more, S2S has multi-language support! It currently supports English, French, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. You can run the pipeline in single-language mode or use the auto flag for automatic language detection. Check out the repo for more details here.

Running Speech-to-Speech requires significant computational resources. Even on a high-end laptop you might encounter latency issues, particularly when using the most advanced models. While a powerful GPU can mitigate these problems, not everyone has the means (or desire!) to set up their own hardware.

This is where Hugging Face's Inference Endpoints (IE) come into play. Inference Endpoints allow you to rent a virtual machine equipped with a GPU (or other hardware you might need) and pay only for the time your system is running, providing an ideal solution for deploying performance-heavy applications like Speech-to-Speech.

In this blog post, we’ll guide you step by step to deploy Speech-to-Speech to a Hugging Face Inference Endpoint. This is what we'll cover:

Inference Endpoints provide a scalable and efficient way to deploy machine learning models. These endpoints allow you to serve models with minimal setup, leveraging a variety of powerful hardware. Inference Endpoints are ideal for deploying applications that require high performance and reliability, without the need to manage underlying infrastructure.

Here's a few key features, and be sure to check out the documentation for more:

Inference Endpoints supports all of the Transformers and Sentence-Transformers tasks, but can also support custom tasks. These are the IE setup options:

For simpler models, options 1 and 2 are ideal and make deploying with Inference Endpoints super straightforward. However, for a complex pipeline like S2S, you will need the flexibility of option 3: deploying our IE using a custom Docker image.

This method not only provides more flexibility but also improved performance by optimizing the build process and gathering necessary data. If you’re dealing with complex model pipelines or want to optimize your application deployment, this guide will offer valuable insights.

To begin creating a custom Docker image, we started by cloning Hugging Face’s default Docker image repository. This serves as a great starting point for deploying machine learning models in inference tasks.

You can check out all of our changes here

With the repository cloned, the next step was tailoring the image to support our Speech-to-Speech pipeline.

To integrate the project smoothly, we added the speech-to-speech codebase and any required datasets as submodules. This approach offers better version control, ensuring the exact version of the code and data is always available when the Docker image is built.

By including data directly within the Docker container, we avoid having to download it each time the endpoint is instantiated, which significantly reduces startup time and ensures the system is reproducible. The data is stored in a Hugging Face repository, which provides easy tracking and versioning.

Next, we modified the Dockerfile to suit our needs:

Once the modifications were in place, we built and pushed the custom image to Docker Hub:

With the Docker image built and pushed, it’s ready to be used in the Hugging Face Inference Endpoint. By using this pre-built image, the endpoint can launch faster and run more efficiently, as all dependencies and data are pre-packaged within the image.

Using a custom docker image just requires a slightly different configuration, feel free to check out the documentation. We will walk through the approach to do this in both the GUI and the API.

The Model Repository doesn't actually matter since the models are specified and downloaded in the container creation, but Inference Endpoints requires a model, so feel free to pick a slim one of your choice.

You need to specify HF_TOKEN because we need to download gated models in the container creation stage. This won't be necessary if you use models that aren't gated or private.

The current huggingface-inference-toolkit entrypoint uses port 5000 as default, but the inference endpoint expects port 80. You should match this in the Container Port. We already set it in our dockerfile, but beware if making your own from scratch!

Here we will walk through the steps for creating the endpoint with the API. Just use this code in your python environment of choice.

Use a token that can write an endpoint (Write or Fine-Grained)

To use the endpoint, we will need to build a small webservice. The code for it is done on s2s_handler.py in the speech_to_speech library which we use for the client and webservice_starlette.py in thespeech_to_speech_inference_toolkit which we used to build the docker image. Normally, you would only have a custom handler for an endpoint, but since we want to have a really low latency, we also built the webservice to support websocket connections instead of normal requests. This sounds intimidating at first, but the webservice is only 32 lines of code!

This code will run prepare_handler on startup, which will initialize all the models and warm them up. Then, each message will be processed by inference_handler.process_streaming_data

This method simply receives the audio data from the client, chunks it into small parts for the VAD, and submits it to a queue for processing. Then it checks the output processing queue (the spoken response from the model!) and returns it if there is something. All of the internal processing is handled by Hugging Face's speech_to_speech library.

The webservice receives and returns audio. But there is still a big missing piece, how do we record and play back the audio? For that, we created a client that connects to the service. The easiest is to divide the analysis in the connection to the webservice and the recording/playing of audio.

Initializing the webservice client requires setting a header for all messages with our Hugging Face Token. When initializing the client, we set what we want to do on common messages (open, close, error, message). This will determine what our client does when the server sends it messages.

We can see that the reactions to the messages are straight forward, with the on_message being the only method with more complexity. This method understands when the server is done responding and starts 'listening' back to the user. Otherwise, it puts the data from the server in the playback queue.

The audio is recorded on the audio_input_callback method, it simply submits all chunks to a queue. Then, it is sent to the server with the send_audio method. Here, if there is no audio to send, we still submit an empty array in order to receive a response from the server. The responses from the server are handled by the on_message method we saw earlier in the blog. Then, the playback of the audio responses are handled by the audio_output_callback method. Here we only need to ensure that the audio is in the range we expect (We don't want to destroy someone eardrum's because of a faulty package!) and ensure that the size of the output array is what the playback library expects.

In this post, we walked through the steps of deploying the Speech-to-Speech (S2S) pipeline on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints using a custom Docker image. We built a custom container to handle the complexities of the S2S pipeline and demonstrated how to configure it for scalable, efficient deployment. Hugging Face Inference Endpoints make it easier to bring performance-heavy applications like Speech-to-Speech to life, without the hassle of managing hardware or infrastructure.

If you're interested in trying it out or have any questions, feel free to explore the following resources:

Have issues or questions? Open a discussion on the relevant GitHub repository, and we’ll be happy to help!

#10896. Releasing Outlines-core 0.1.0: structured generation in Rust and Python

dottxt and Hugging Face are excited to announce that we have been collaborating on outlines-core, a Rust port of outlines’s core algorithms for structured generation. On top of getting reliable output from LLMs with outlines, this Rust port offers several further benefits to users of outlines:

These improvements should not only improve the performance for existing outlines users, but also dramatically increase the ways users can incorporate structured generation into their LLM workflows. outlines-core is now public, integrated in outlines, and the version 0.1.0 of the Python bindings are out. You can find the repo here.

Structured generation means that your LLM is guaranteed to follow a desired format. This could be JSON, a Pydantic Model, a regular expression or a context-free grammar. The key is that structured generation forbids the 'wrong' tokens from being generated.

Let’s take an extremely simple example. The LLM should generate a boolean, “true” or “false”. And nothing more. For the sake of illustration, let’s say that LLMs generate characters instead of tokens. So the first character is ", we can just skip the forward pass. For the second, we don’t need to sample from all possible characters. The LLM should just choose between t or f.

After that, regardless of the path we take, there is only one valid next character. If the LLM chose t as the first character, then it has to follow with r, u and e. And similarly if it chose f it follows with a, l, s, e. And will choose the last " as the final character regardless of the path. There is of course more under the hood, for more in-depth coverage we recommend this dottxt blog and the associated paper on arxiv.

It might not immediately be obvious how amazing structured generation can be. The first use-case many think of is “nice, now my LLM can return valid JSON, so I can treat it as an API and serialize/deserialize JSON reliably”. But that’s just scratching the surface. When you think about it, structure is everywhere, even in places where you least expect it like the GSM8K benchmark.

These are just a few examples of what structured generation enables:

And, perhaps more surprising, it reduces the sensitivity of evaluations to the specific prompt being used and the number of shots. Apart from the amazing tricks that structure gives you, it’s also more performant. The dottxt blog has many good articles with performance benchmarks.

Probably the first thing that comes to your mind when you hear “rewrite in Rust” is performance. And yes, that’s the case for outlines-core as well. Several key parts are yet to be moved over to Rust, and despite that, we already see an average 2x improvement in compilation speed.

Before the Rust port, Outlines used Numba to accelerate the building of the index. While Numba is fast (the runtime performance is comparable to Rust), the JIT-compilation of the Numba functions added a source of latency during the first run, which was a source of frustration for many users. Using Rust means we can compile the index building functions ahead of time, adding no latency during the first run. While this was not important in a production context (since the first run could anyways be done as part of deployment), it can make a huge difference during the experimentation phase!

One of the main reasons for rewriting Outlines in Rust is the emphasis on safety and reliability that Rust brings to the table. Rust's strong static typing, combined with Rust's ownership model, eliminate entire classes of bugs, such as null pointer dereferences and data races in concurrent code. This leads to more robust and secure software.

In the context of Outlines, safety is crucial. Structured generation often involves complex data structures and manipulations, especially when dealing with high-performance inference engines. By leveraging Rust's safety guarantees, we reduce the risk of runtime errors and undefined behaviors that can arise from memory mismanagement.

Additionally, Rust's compile-time checks encourage developers to write cleaner and more maintainable code. This improves the current codebase and makes future development more efficient. New contributors can onboard more quickly, and the code is easier to audit and verify for correctness.

Outlines was designed to do more than providing the core algorithms for structured generation. Among other things, it includes integrations to other libraries like transformers which mean the library packs many dependencies. Separating the core algorithms from the Outlines library means that other libraries wishing to include structured generation can do so by importing a very lightweight library. So we can imagine in the near future libraries such as transformers and llama-cpp-python integrating structured generation directly. This allows the dottxt team to focus on the core algorithms.

Most of LLM training is written in Python, but inference is slightly different. It happens on many different devices, on specialized servers and is written in a range of programming languages. This is why portability also matters for structured generation. By having the core functionality of outlines written in rust, we can now create bindings to other languages.

For example, this port makes the integration into the text-generation-inference much smoother. TGI’s server logic is written in Rust, and we want to avoid having to call Python code as much as we possibly can. It also means libraries like mistral.rs or models implemented using candle can benefit from Outlines’s performance and capabilities.

In the future we plan to explore bindings to JS/TS, allowing outlines to be used in transformers-js. Or potentially Swift bindings, making outlines natively usable on Apple devices. But for now the focus is going to be on the Python bindings, and continuing to make outlines-core’s feature set complete by expanding support for the JSON Schema specification.

Do you like working with structured generation, parsers, making LLMs output only valid JSON? Star the library, tweet about it, join in and contribute! Share your work on Twitter, and with dottxt’s and Hugging Face's community.

#10895. Building Accessible Navigation Menus with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Navigation is one of the most important components of a website. It helps visitors discover content, move between pages, and understand how a site is organized. However, a navigation menu that works well with a mouse may create problems for keyboard users, people who rely on screen readers, or visitors using small mobile screens.

Building an accessible navigation menu involves more than adding a few ARIA attributes or increasing the size of clickable elements. Developers need to consider semantic HTML, keyboard interaction, visible focus indicators, responsive layouts, and predictable behavior.

In this tutorial, we will build a responsive navigation menu using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We will also examine common accessibility mistakes and explain how to test the finished component.

HTML provides several native elements that communicate the purpose and structure of a navigation interface.

A website's primary navigation should generally use a

element containing a list of links. This structure helps browsers and assistive technologies identify the navigation region and understand the available destinations.

The aria-label gives the navigation landmark a descriptive name. This becomes particularly useful when a page contains multiple navigation regions, such as a primary menu and a footer menu.

Using a list also communicates that the links form a related group. Each link has a meaningful destination, making it possible for visitors to navigate the site without relying on visual positioning alone.

A common mistake is using clickable

elements instead of links. Although JavaScript can make a div respond to clicks, it does not automatically provide the same keyboard behavior and navigation semantics as an anchor element.

For navigation to another page, use an anchor. For an action that changes the interface, use a button.

A navigation menu should adapt to the available screen width without hiding important links or creating horizontal scrolling.

The following CSS creates a flexible desktop navigation layout:

Flexbox aligns the logo and navigation horizontally while allowing the link list to wrap when necessary.

The gap property controls the spacing between links without requiring individual margins. Removing the list markers also produces a cleaner navigation layout while preserving the underlying list semantics.

Notice that the hover style includes an underline as well as a color change. This provides an additional visual cue instead of relying exclusively on color.

However, hover effects alone are insufficient because touchscreens do not have conventional hover behavior, and keyboard users do not navigate with a mouse.

Many visitors use the Tab key to move between interactive elements. A navigation menu should make the currently focused link easy to identify.

The :focus-visible pseudo-class allows browsers to display a focus indicator when it is appropriate, particularly during keyboard navigation.

Avoid removing the browser's default outline unless you replace it with a clearly visible alternative.

Keyboard accessibility also depends on the HTML structure. Standard anchor elements already support keyboard focus and activation, so the basic navigation above does not need custom JavaScript keyboard handlers.

That is an important design principle: use native browser behavior wherever possible rather than recreating it unnecessarily.

On smaller screens, a horizontal navigation menu may occupy too much space. A toggle button can provide a compact alternative while preserving access to the links.

The menu button is hidden on larger screens and displayed on smaller ones. On mobile, the navigation links are initially hidden until JavaScript adds the is-open class.

The aria-expanded attribute communicates whether the menu is currently expanded, while aria-controls identifies the element controlled by the button.

These attributes must reflect the actual interface state. Adding them without updating their values when the menu opens and closes can confuse assistive technology users.

The JavaScript should update both the visual state and the accessibility information when the user activates the button.

When the button is clicked, the code reads the current state, reverses it, updates aria-expanded, and toggles the CSS class.

Because the button is a native HTML button, it already supports keyboard activation. There is no need to add separate Enter or Space key handlers.

For a production implementation, you should also consider what happens when the viewport changes from mobile to desktop. For example, if the menu is open on mobile and the visitor resizes the browser, the desktop layout should not remain in an inconsistent state.

A more complete implementation can synchronize the menu state with the responsive breakpoint, close the menu when a navigation link is selected, and ensure that hidden links cannot be reached through keyboard navigation.

A navigation menu may look correct and still be difficult to use. Testing should cover both automated checks and real interactions.

Start with keyboard testing. Use Tab and Shift+Tab to move through the logo, menu button, and navigation links. Check that focus indicators are visible and that the order follows the visual and logical structure.

The menu button appears at the intended breakpoint.

Activating the button opens and closes the navigation.

The aria-expanded value matches the visible state.

Hidden links are not available for keyboard interaction while the menu is closed.

Selecting a link takes the visitor to the correct destination.

You can also use accessibility inspection tools to identify missing accessible names, invalid ARIA attributes, and other common problems.

Automated tools are useful, but they cannot establish that every interaction is understandable. Manual testing with a keyboard and, where possible, a screen reader remains important.

For larger websites, reusable navigation components and automated browser tests can help prevent accessibility regressions when styles or interaction logic change.

Accessible navigation starts with semantic HTML and builds on that foundation through responsive CSS, visible focus indicators, and carefully implemented JavaScript.

Native links and buttons provide much of the expected keyboard behavior automatically. Responsive styles make the menu usable across screen sizes, while accurate ARIA state helps communicate whether a collapsible menu is open or closed.

The most reliable approach is to keep the implementation as simple as possible, use browser features instead of recreating them, and test the actual experience rather than relying only on how the interface looks.

When accessibility is considered from the beginning, navigation becomes easier to maintain and more usable for a wider range of visitors.

#10893. Transformers.js v3: WebGPU Support, New Models & Tasks, and More…

After more than a year of development, we're excited to announce the release of 🤗 Transformers.js v3!

You can get started by installing Transformers.js v3 from NPM using:

For more information, check out the documentation.

WebGPU is a new web standard for accelerated graphics and compute. The API enables web developers to use the underlying system's GPU to carry out high-performance computations directly in the browser. WebGPU is the successor to WebGL and provides significantly better performance, because it allows for more direct interaction with modern GPUs. Lastly, it supports general-purpose GPU computations, which makes it just perfect for machine learning!

As of October 2024, global WebGPU support is around 70% (according to caniuse.com), meaning some users may not be able to use the API.

If the following demos do not work in your browser, you may need to enable it using a feature flag:

Thanks to our collaboration with ONNX Runtime Web, enabling WebGPU acceleration is as simple as setting device: 'webgpu' when loading a model. Let's see some examples!

Example: Compute text embeddings on WebGPU (demo)

Example: Perform automatic speech recognition with OpenAI whisper on WebGPU (demo)

Example: Perform image classification with MobileNetV4 on WebGPU (demo)

Before Transformers.js v3, we used the quantized option to specify whether to use a quantized (q8) or full-precision (fp32) variant of the model by setting quantized to true or false, respectively. Now, we've added the ability to select from a much larger list with the dtype parameter.

The list of available quantizations depends on the model, but some common ones are: full-precision ("fp32"), half-precision ("fp16"), 8-bit ("q8", "int8", "uint8"), and 4-bit ("q4", "bnb4", "q4f16").

(e.g., mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-xsmall-v1)

Example: Run Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct in 4-bit quantization (demo)

Some encoder-decoder models, like Whisper or Florence-2, are extremely sensitive to quantization settings: especially of the encoder. For this reason, we added the ability to select per-module dtypes, which can be done by providing a mapping from module name to dtype.

This release increases the total number of supported architectures to 120 (see full list), spanning a wide range of input modalities and tasks. Notable new names include: Phi-3, Gemma & Gemma 2, LLaVa, Moondream, Florence-2, MusicGen, Sapiens, Depth Pro, PyAnnote, and RT-DETR.

As part of the release, we've published 25 new example projects and templates, primarily focused on showcasing WebGPU support! This includes demos like Phi-3.5 WebGPU and Whisper WebGPU, as shown below.

We're in the process of moving all our example projects and demos to https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js-examples, so stay tuned for updates on this!

As of today's release, the community has converted over 1200 models to be compatible with Transformers.js! You can find the full list of available models here.

If you'd like to convert your own models or fine-tunes, you can use our conversion script as follows:

After uploading the generated files to the Hugging Face Hub, remember to add the transformers.js tag so others can easily find and use your model!

Transformers.js v3 is now compatible with the three most popular server-side JavaScript runtimes:

Finally, we're delighted to announce that Transformers.js will now be published under the official Hugging Face organization on NPM as @huggingface/transformers (instead of @xenova/transformers, which was used for v1 and v2).

We've also moved the repository to the official Hugging Face organization on GitHub (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js), which will be our new home — come say hi! We look forward to hearing your feedback, responding to your issues, and reviewing your PRs!

This is a significant milestone and we're extremely grateful to the community for helping us achieve this long-term goal! None of this would be possible without all of you… thank you! 🤗

#10892. Hugging Face Teams Up with Protect AI: Enhancing Model Security for the ML Community

We are pleased to announce our partnership with Protect AI, as part of our long-standing commitment to provide a safe and reliable platform for the ML community.

Protect AI is a company founded with a mission to create a safer AI-powered world. They are developing powerful tools, namely Guardian, to ensure that the rapid pace of AI innovation can continue without compromising security.

Our decision to partner with Protect AI stems from their community driven approach to security, active support of open source, and expertise in all things security x AI.

Interested in joining our security partnership / providing scanning information on the Hub? Please get in touch with us over at security@huggingface.co.

To share models, we serialize weights, configs and other data structures we use to interact with the models, in order to facilitate storage and transport. Some serialization formats are vulnerable to nasty exploits, such as arbitrary code execution (looking at you pickle), making shared models that use those formats potentially dangerous.

As Hugging Face has become a popular platform for model sharing, we’d like to help protect the community from this, hence why we have developed tools like picklescan and why we are integrating Guardian in our scanner suite.

Pickle is not the only exploitable format out there, see for reference how one can exploit Keras Lambda layers to achieve arbitrary code execution. The good news is that Guardian catches both of these exploits and more in additional file formats – see their Knowledge Base for up to date scanner information.

Read all our documentation on security here: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/security 🔥

While integrating Guardian as a third-party scanner, we have used this as an opportunity to revamp our frontend to display scan results. Here is what it now looks like:

As you can see from the screenshot, there's nothing you have to do to benefit from this! All public model repositories will be scanned by Guardian automatically as soon as you push your files to the Hub. Here is an example repository you can check out to see the feature in action: mcpotato/42-eicar-street.

Note that you might not see a scan for your model as of today, as we have over 1 million model repos. It may take us some time to catch up 😅.

In total, we have already scanned hundreds of millions of files, because we believe that empowering the community to share models in a safe and frictionless manner will lead to growth for the whole field.

#10891. CinePile 2.0 - making stronger datasets with adversarial refinement

In this blog post we share the journey of releasing CinePile 2.0, a significantly improved version of our long video QA dataset. The improvements in the new dataset rely on a new approach that we coined adversarial dataset refinement.

We're excited to share both CinePile 2.0 and our adversarial refinement method implementation, which we believe can strengthen many existing datasets and directly be part of future dataset creation pipelines.

If you are mainly interested in the adversarial refinement method, you can jump directly to the Adversarial Refinement section.

In May 2024, we launched CinePile, a long video QA dataset with about 300,000 training samples and 5,000 test samples.

The first release stood out from other datasets in two aspects:

Part of the secret sauce behind it is that it relies on movie clips from YouTube and Q&A distilled from precise audio descriptions designed for visually impaired audiences. These descriptions offer rich context beyond basic visuals (e.g., "What color is the car?"), helping us create more complex questions.

To automate question creation, we first built question templates by inspecting existing datasets like MovieQA and TVQA. We clustered the questions in these datasets using a textual similarity model WhereIsAI/UAE-Large-V1 and then prompted GPT-4 with 10 random examples from each cluster to generate a question template and a prototypical question for each:

Since templates aren't always relevant to every movie clip, we used Gemini 1.0 Pro to select the most appropriate ones for each scene. Next, we feed a language model the scene's text, selected template names (e.g., "Physical Possession"), sample questions, and a system prompt to create scene-specific questions. A well-designed prompt helps the model focus on the entire scene, generating deeper questions while avoiding superficial ones. We found that:

Using this approach, we generate approximately 32 questions per video. Prior to releasing CinePile, we implemented several mechanisms to ensure the quality of the dataset/benchmark that we cover in the next section.

While our process typically generates well-formed, answerable questions, some turn out to be trivial or rely on basic concepts that don't require watching the clip. To address this, we used several large language models (LLMs) to identify and filter three types of issues:

Through continued use of the benchmark by our team and the broader community, we identified several areas for improvement that drove us to consider CinePile 2.0.

For CinePile's second release, we worked together with Hugging Face (following their successful experimentation with fine-tuning Video Llava 7B on CinePile) to identify and prioritize several areas of improvement.

While the degeneracy filtering was useful in CinePile 1.0, it had several limitations:

To address these issues, we introduced a new Adversarial Refinement pipeline that helps improve weak questions rather than simply discarding them. This approach can be more easily applied at scale. Throughout this post, we'll refer to the model(s) that identify degenerate questions (using only the question and answer choices, without visual or dialogue information) as the "Deaf-Blind LLM."

The Adversarial Refinement pipeline aims to modify questions or answers until a Deaf-Blind LLM cannot easily predict the correct answer. Here's how it works:

Given the computational demands of this iterative process, we needed a powerful yet accessible LLM that could run locally to avoid API usage limits, delays, and cloud service costs. We chose:

Briefly, this was the impact of running adversarial refinement in CinePile:

In this release, we're publishing both our adversarial refinement pipeline and the code for identifying weak questions. The complete implementation, including all prompts, is available in our public repository.

After testing both previously evaluated models and 16 new Video-LLMs on the modified test set, we’ve highlighted the top performers in the figure below. Here’s what the results show:

Gemini 1.5 Pro led among commercial Vision Language Models (VLMs)

GPT-based models showed competitive performance

Gemini 1.5 Flash, a lighter version of Gemini 1.5 Pro

The open-source video-LLM community has made significant progress from the first to the current release of CinePile. This is what we learned:

LLaVa-One Vision leads open-source models

Smaller models showed competitive performance

The hard-split results in CinePile clearly demonstrate that current models still lag far behind human capability in understanding visual narratives and story elements. This gap highlights the value of CinePile's new release as a benchmark for measuring progress toward more sophisticated visual understanding.

#10890. What “Clear Form” Should Really Do: Managing Draft Data in JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A user fills out a form, requests a preview, and then changes their mind. They click “Clear,” the inputs become empty, and the interface appears ready for someone else.

A moment later, the previous preview returns.

The application cleared the fields, but an asynchronous request still held the old values and updated the screen when it finished. Similar problems occur when drafts remain in browser storage, validation messages retain personal details, or a component’s internal state survives a visual reset.

For developers building onboarding, expense, application, and document workflows, clearing a form is a state-management operation. It deserves the same attention as submission.

This article explains how to define that operation, prevent stale results, and inspect the outcome using practical browser and testing tools.

Start by listing the places where a draft exists. The visible inputs are only one location.

When reviewing a financial-data interface, a useful design exercise is to map which information belongs to the current draft and what should happen when the user starts again. The same exercise applies to expense submissions and customer onboarding; the implementation must be assessed separately from the visible interface.

Name actions according to their actual scope. “Clear this form” should not imply that previously submitted records have been deleted. If a draft has been saved remotely, distinguish clearing the current screen from deleting the saved draft.

For a broader introduction to form structure and validation, SitePoint’s guide to modern HTML forms provides useful background.

Autosave is convenient, but persisting the entire form after every keystroke is an architectural decision, not a harmless UI enhancement.

For a short workflow, keeping the draft in memory may be sufficient. For a longer workflow, decide which fields may be retained, how the user understands that behavior, and when the retained copy is removed.

Browser storage options have different lifetimes. According to MDN’s sessionStorage documentation, session storage is associated with a page session and survives reloads. It should not be treated as equivalent to an ordinary variable that disappears when the page reloads.

Nor does shorter retention make storage a security boundary. The OWASP HTML5 security guidance cautions against storing sensitive information in local storage because JavaScript running in the origin can access it.

This reduces unnecessary copies. It does not provide secure memory erasure or protect a page from every script that can access its data.

The native form.reset() method restores controls to their default values. It does not necessarily make every field empty.

For example, an input rendered with a default value can return to that value after a reset. The method also does not clear a separate preview element, invalidate a network response, or update every framework-managed state variable.

Use a small HTML form with empty defaults for the following example:

The clear control uses type="button" so the application can coordinate the complete operation.

In a React or Vue implementation, apply the same policy to the state that controls the inputs. Clearing the DOM while leaving the component state intact can cause the old values to reappear.

Cancellation helps reduce unnecessary work, but request identity is what protects the interface from a stale result.

Assign each request a generation number. Whenever the draft changes or is cleared, advance that number. A response may update the UI only if its number still matches the current generation.

The following JavaScript works with the HTML above. It assumes a same-origin POST /api/preview endpoint that accepts JSON and returns {"summary":"plain text"}. That endpoint is an integration requirement; it is not implemented here.

Editing a field also invalidates the preview. Otherwise, users could mistake a result based on earlier values for a result based on their current input.

The code writes server-provided text with textContent rather than interpreting it as HTML. It also displays a fixed failure message instead of echoing request values into an error.

AbortController allows the client to abort fetch-related work. Aborting a browser request does not guarantee that server processing stopped or that data already received by the server was deleted.

The generation check enforces the narrower promise: obsolete work must not update this interface. SitePoint’s introduction to the Fetch API explains the request and response mechanics behind the example.

The example intentionally does not save drafts. If your application does, add cleanup to the clear operation rather than assuming that resetting the form handles it.

Remove the application’s specific draft entry. Avoid localStorage.clear() as a general cleanup shortcut, since it also removes unrelated keys for that origin.

Keep the UI honest if storage cleanup fails. Do not announce that every saved copy is gone when the application has only emptied the visible controls.

An object URL should be revoked when it is no longer needed, but revoking it does not delete a file the user already downloaded.

For programmatic changes, call the same invalidation function used by input events. Assigning an input’s value in JavaScript does not automatically trigger the user-input event handler.

You do not need a large dependency stack to verify a clear operation. Each of these tools answers a different question.

Chrome’s local-storage inspection guide explains how to inspect stored entries. Check session storage and IndexedDB too if the application uses them; an empty local-storage table is not proof that no browser persistence exists.

Mock Service Worker is useful for creating reproducible response conditions during development. Use fictional fixtures so debugging sessions do not depend on real personal records.

With Playwright network interception, hold a preview response until the test explicitly releases it. Fill the form, request a preview, clear the draft, and only then release the response. Assert that the input remains empty and the preview never returns.

A controlled release is more reliable than hoping a fixed delay creates the right race. Also test two requests completing in reverse order.

A useful review checks the operation at several points:

Supplement automated accessibility checks with keyboard and screen-reader testing. The Playwright accessibility guide explains that automated checks detect only some accessibility problems.

Verify backend behavior separately. Server validation, authorization, retention, and deletion require their own implementation and tests. A clean browser interface cannot demonstrate those guarantees.

A reliable clear operation has a defined scope. It invalidates pending work, resets the application’s draft state, removes derived output, and handles persistence according to the product’s stated behavior.

The implementation can remain small. What matters is that the team knows where draft data lives and tests what happens when events arrive in an inconvenient order.

When developers make those boundaries explicit, “Clear form” becomes a predictable action rather than a visual reset that leaves the previous workflow running.

#10888. Introducing SynthID Text

Do you find it difficult to tell if text was written by a human or generated by AI? Being able to identify AI-generated content is essential to promoting trust in information, and helping to address problems such as misattribution and misinformation. Today, Google DeepMind and Hugging Face are excited to launch SynthID Text in Transformers v4.46.0, releasing later today. This technology allows you to apply watermarks to AI-generated text using a logits processor for generation tasks, and detect those watermarks with a classifier.

Check out the SynthID Text paper in Nature for the complete technical details of this algorithm, and Google’s Responsible GenAI Toolkit for more on how to apply SynthID Text in your products.

The primary goal of SynthID Text is to encode a watermark into AI-generated text in a way that helps you determine if text was generated from your LLM without affecting how the underlying LLM works or negatively impacting generation quality. Google DeepMind has developed a watermarking technique that uses a pseudo-random function, called a g-function, to augment the generation process of any LLM such that the watermark is imperceptible to humans but is visible to a trained model. This has been implemented as a generation utility that is compatible with any LLM without modification using the model.generate() API, along with an end-to-end example of how to train detectors to recognize watermarked text. Check out the research paper that has more complete details about the SynthID Text algorithm.

Watermarks are configured using a dataclass that parameterizes the g-function and how it is applied in the tournament sampling process. Each model you use should have its own watermarking configuration that should be stored securely and privately, otherwise your watermark may be replicable by others.

You must define two parameters in every watermarking configuration:

The keys parameter is a list integers that are used to compute g-function scores across the model's vocabulary. Using 20 to 30 unique, randomly generated numbers is recommended to balance detectability against generation quality.

The ngram_len parameter is used to balance robustness and detectability; the larger the value the more detectable the watermark will be, at the cost of being more brittle to changes. A good default value is 5, but it needs to be at least 2.

You can further configure the watermark based on your performance needs. See the SynthIDTextWatermarkingConfig class for more information.

The research paper includes additional analyses of how specific configuration values affect watermark performance.

Applying a watermark is a straightforward change to your existing generation calls. Once you define your configuration, pass a SynthIDTextWatermarkingConfig object as the watermarking_config= parameter to model.generate() and all generated text will carry the watermark. Check out the SynthID Text Space for an interactive example of watermark application, and see if you can tell.

Watermarks are designed to be detectable by a trained classifier but imperceptible to humans. Every watermarking configuration you use with your models needs to have a detector trained to recognize the mark.

A Bayesian detector class is provided in Transformers, along with an end-to-end example of how to train a detector to recognize watermarked text using a specific watermarking configuration. Models that use the same tokenizer can also share watermarking configuration and detector, thus sharing a common watermark, so long as the detector's training set includes examples from all models that share a watermark.

This trained detector can be uploaded to a private HF Hub to make it accessible across your organization. Google’s Responsible GenAI Toolkit has more on how to productionize SynthID Text in your products.

SynthID Text watermarks are robust to some transformations, such as cropping pieces of text, modifying a few words, or mild paraphrasing, but this method does have limitations.

SynthID Text is not built to directly stop motivated adversaries from causing harm. However, it can make it harder to use AI-generated content for malicious purposes, and it can be combined with other approaches to give better coverage across content types and platforms.

The authors would like to thank Robert Stanforth and Tatiana Matejovicova for their contributions to this work.

Watermarking LLM-generated text with SynthID Text

#10887. A Deepdive into Aya Expanse: Advancing the Frontier of Multilinguality

This is a guest blog post by the Cohere For AI team. Cohere For AI is Cohere's research lab that seeks to solve complex machine learning problems.

With the release of the Aya Expanse family, featuring 8B and 32B parameter models, we are addressing one of the most urgent challenges in AI: the lack of highly performant multilingual models that can rival the capabilities of monolingual ones. While AI has made tremendous progress, there remains a stark gap in the performance of models across multiple languages. Aya Expanse is the result of several years of dedicated research at C4AI --- data arbitrage, multilingual preference training, safety tuning, and model merging.

These combined breakthroughs have resulted in new state-of-the-art performance on multilingual. We evaluate our models on a set of evaluations including the Arena-Hard-Auto dataset (paper), translated to the 23 languages which we release for others to use. In pairwise comparison, Aya Expanse 32B outperforms Gemma 2 27B, Mistral 8x22B, and Llama 3.1 70B, a model more than 2x its size, setting a new state-of-the-art for multilingual performance. We also release Aya Expanse 8B, which outperforms the leading open-weights models in its parameter class such as Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, and the recently released Ministral 8B with win rates ranging from 60.4% to 70.6%. We observe even larger gains across less challenging evals.

We release both models as open weights for the research community, and hope it will further accelerate multilingual progress. In this blog post, we share technical details behind each of the key algorithmic components used in the training pipeline.

The use of synthetic data – data generated by an expert or “teacher” model to train another model – has become increasingly central to the development of LLMs, particularly as model training has exhausted current data sources. However, for multilingual data, especially with low-resource languages, there are few good examples of teacher models, creating an extra added challenge to leveraging synthetic data. Furthermore, recent research has suggested that an over-reliance on synthetic data leads to model collapse.

In our recent work we demonstrate that these limitations can be addressed through “data arbitrage” – strategically sampling from a pool of teacher models. This approach has important implications as it challenges the traditional reliance on a single-teacher model for generating synthetic data. Instead, data arbitrage leverages performance variations among a pool of models. Although this technique is applicable to any domain, it is particularly suited to the multilingual setting, where the absence of a universally effective teacher that excels across all languages presents significant challenges In the creation of high-quality synthetic multilingual datasets, multilingual arbitrage proves valuable by utilizing a diverse pool of models to strategically sample different parts of the data distribution for improved multilingual generations.

We first train a model pool for groups of languages and employ an Arbiter to evaluate and select the optimal generation. The Arbiter here is an internal reward model (RM) to score the model generations. In Reward-Based Routing, for each prompt in a given language, we generate completions from all models in the pool and score them using the reward model. The completion with the highest score is chosen as the final completion for that prompt. Our 8B model, even at the SFT stage trained with Multilingual Arbitrage, had over 9.1% improvement in win-rate measured against Gemma 2 9B compared to the previous Aya 23 model, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in leveraging diverse model strengths across languages.

Following supervised fine-tuning, alignment to human preferences is a key step for training today’s state-of-the-art LLMs. Although heavily adopted, it is known that preference training is already challenging in a monolingual setting. Maximizing gains from preference training in a multilingual setting introduces even more challenges. The vast majority of existing preference datasets are exclusively English and the few existing multilingual preference datasets are often of low-quality. Moreover, modeling many diverse languages simultaneously is known to be a difficult optimization problem where naively optimizing for performance in some languages often leads to regressions in performance in other languages.

In LHF Can Speak Many Languages: Unlocking Multilingual Preference Optimization for LLMs, we leverage a novel synthetic data generation technique to construct high-quality multilingual preference data pairs by contrasting in-language completions from a highly performant multilingual LLM with lower quality completions translated from English which were generated by a weaker model. This steers our model away from generating low-quality multilingual completions which often contain undesirable artifacts, such as those introduced by poor translation. We show that this method unlocks substantial gains in performance across all languages and often also results in gains for languages not included in the preference training data.

While this work also shows that preference training with online data outperforms its offline variant, during training of Aya Expanse, we found that the combination of first preference-training with offline data followed by preference-training with online data to be better than either online or offline training alone. In the first preference training stage, we train on data curated by taking the highest and lowest reward responses from the Arbitrage stage as the chosen and rejected completions, which makes the first stage of DPO training offline.

After offline preference training, we run online iterative DPO, where we sample multiple online generations for each prompt from the model trained during the last iteration, rank these generations with a Reward Model, and then further train on these preference pairs. For both models, we repeat this process for 3 iterations as we found that going beyond 3 iterations led to minimal gains at the cost of additional re-tuning parameters like regularization coefficient (beta) and sometimes introduced reward hacking behavior. Overall, for Aya Expanse 8B, the combination of offline and online preference training on top of the model trained with arbitrage, led to 7.1% additional gains in win rate against Gemma 2 9B.

A reappearing problem throughout any post-training (and pre-training) pipeline, whether it consists of a single stage such as SFT, or a more complex multi-stage optimization pipeline, such as our pipeline above, is choosing the right data mixtures for training. The intricacies of this process demand considerable effort in fine-tuning hyperparameters and data combinations. Merging multiple models is an alternative approach for enabling complex multi-tasking at a reduced aggregate computational cost. In Aya Expanse, we directly build on the findings of our recent research paper Mix Data or Merge Models? Optimizing for Diverse Multi-Task Learning and apply merging in both the Arbitrage phase, and at each iteration of preference training.

When training multiple separate models with the goal of merging, it is important to maximize diversity between checkpoints. However, this should be balanced with ensuring that each individual model within the pool achieves high performance. To balance these objectives, we maximize diversity between checkpoints by training models for different language families. This takes advantage of cross-lingual transfer which often provides significant performance benefits while ensuring that linguistic differences provide sufficient differentiation between checkpoints.

Naively, one could split-train a model for each language and then merge, but this does not achieve the same benefits we observe from cross-lingual transfer. To improve robustness in merging, we include some shared languages across each cluster (here English, Spanish, and French). In the final recipe, we used multiple stages of merging runs trained on different clusters of data, and checkpoints within the same run.

In addition to weighted linear averaging, we experiment with multiple merging techniques, namely SLERP, TIES-merging, and DARE-TIES. However, we found weighted averaging to be the most consistent method. As a result, we use weighted averaging throughout the pipeline. Interestingly, we observed significantly larger gains from merging at the 35B scale compared to the 8B scale – up to 3x. This is inline with recent work suggesting merging to be more effective at scale.

These diagrams show our end-to-end post-training pipeline, which resulted in the step-by-step gains discussed earlier. It is truly special to look back and see how far the Aya model series has come, since its inception with Aya 101 accompanied by the Aya Collection, which stretched the limits of open-source collaboration, to now which combines steady progress in key open fundamental research questions to set a new standard for multilingual performance.

This work wouldn’t have been possible without the core Aya Expanse team: Madeline Smith, Marzieh Fadaee, Ahmet Üstün, Beyza Ermis, Sara Hooker, John Dang, Shivalika Singh, Arash Ahmadian, Daniel D'souza, Alejandro Salamanca, Aidan Peppin, Arielle Bailey, Meor Amer, Sungjin Hong, Manoj Govindassamy, Sandra Kublik.

It also wouldn’t have been possible without the wider Cohere For AI and Cohere team. Special thanks to Acyr Locatelli, Adrien Morisot, Jon Ander Campos, Sara Elsharkawy, Eddie Kim, Julia Kreutzer, Nick Frosst, Aidan Gomez, Ivan Zhang.

A huge thanks also goes to our research community – the 220 language ambassadors from around the world who have been part of this release. Thank you to Sree Harsha Nelaturu, Bhavnick Minhas, Christopher Klamm, Isabella Bicalho Frazeto who contributed notebooks that are accessible on the model Hugging Face cards.

Special thank you to Hugging Face for helping make this come together: Omar Sanseviero, Pedro Cuenca, Vaibhav Srivastav, Lysandre Debut, Aritra Roy Gosthipaty.

#10886. Best AI Brand Mention Tracking Tools for Enterprises in 2026: 6 Tools Compared

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

At a large company, the hard part of buying an AI brand mention tracking tool is procurement. IT asks about single sign-on, legal asks where the data sits, and the marketing team that wanted the tool waits weeks to log in. A pilot on one brand in one market looks cheap, then the other markets, the other teams and SSO arrive and the quote looks nothing like the trial.

That is why a generic "best tools" list helps enterprise buyers less than it should. All the tools below track how often ChatGPT, Gemini and Google's AI answers name your brand. What separates them at enterprise size is everything around the tracking: how many people can log in, how logins are controlled, whether the data can leave the tool and whether it copes with ten markets instead of one.

This guide compares six tools on those points. Peec AI ranks first because it combines unlimited users, enforceable SSO, source-level analysis and a published price ladder. The other five suit different buying situations.

AI brand mention tracking measures how often, where and how favourably AI engines name your brand when buyers ask category questions. A tool runs a fixed prompt set daily across engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot, then reports mention rate (visibility), position inside the answer, sentiment, share of voice against competitors and the sources each answer cited.

For an enterprise, the answers differ by engine, country and product line, and a single visibility number hides most of that. Similarweb's May 2026 figures put ChatGPT at 53.9% of AI chatbot web visits, Gemini at 27.9% and Claude at 9.2%, against roughly 76% for ChatGPT in June 2025. The question "what does AI say about us?" is now spread over at least three engines.

Access and identity. Ask how many users each plan allows, whether SSO is available and on which plan, and whether you can enforce it. Most tools put SSO on their top tier or a custom plan, so budget for an enterprise contract early.

Markets and brands. Check whether the price grows per country, language or brand. Ten markets multiply a prompt set quickly.

Data access. The data has to reach the reporting leadership already reads: CSV export, an API, a BI connector or an MCP server.

Source analysis. A mention rate shows where you stand. Source data shows why, by listing the pages each engine read. Without it you cannot tell whether you are missing because nobody writes about you or because your own pages are not picked up.

Prompt volume and engines. A hundred to a hundred and fifty prompts per brand and market is a realistic start. Check which engines each plan includes and which sit behind add-ons.

Cost at your real workload. Price the tool for the users, markets and prompts you will have in a year, not for the pilot.

Enterprise teams rarely run on the entry tier, so the tables below price two realistic workloads: about 150 prompts, and about 350 prompts on ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode with 15 users, both tracked daily on three engines. Price per prompt is the monthly price divided by the prompts the plan includes. Rankscale and AthenaHQ price by answers or credits instead, so Rankscale's rows use the answer volume the workload needs: 150 prompts on three engines over 30 days is 13,500 answers a month, and 350 prompts is 31,500. Profound does not publish prices and is left out of the tables. Treat every figure as directional: enterprise contracts are custom and billed annually, so published self-serve prices show where a negotiation starts, not what you will pay.

Peec AI has the lowest price per prompt in the first table and the lowest monthly price in the second. Scrunch AI's Core plan costs $2.00 per prompt at 125 prompts and five users, and its larger plans are quote-only. Against Rankscale, the only other tool here with a published enterprise price, Peec AI costs 36% less at 150 prompts ($245 against $385) and 37% less at 350 prompts ($495 against $780). Rankscale does include more engines in its price, which Peec AI reserves for Enterprise. On ChatGPT plus both Google surfaces with 15 people logging in, Peec AI is the cheapest of the tools priced in these tables: $495 against $638 for Otterly.AI once Google AI Mode is added, and $780 for Rankscale. Otterly.AI and Rankscale include more engines in their price.

One thing changes these tables: single sign-on. Peec AI, Profound, AthenaHQ, Scrunch AI and Otterly.AI put SSO on Enterprise, and Rankscale puts it on a custom plan. If IT requires SSO, every tool here becomes a quote, and the published prices only show where the negotiation starts. Annual billing takes 15% to 17% off most of these.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform with a New York office. It tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice, breaks every answer into the sources the engine read and turns the gaps it finds into prioritised actions. At enterprise scale its pricing is the main difference: users are unlimited on every plan, and Peec does not charge per country or language, with multi-country tracking from the Advanced plan.

Best for: Enterprise teams that want one tool for every market and every team, and need to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Profound suits purchases that have to clear an information security review before anything else. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise, and it raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026, which settles the vendor-risk question quickly.

Best for: Companies where compliance and vendor risk decide the purchase.

AthenaHQ was built by two former Google Search and DeepMind engineers. Its Enterprise plan has the longest feature list of the quote-based tools: SAML and OIDC single sign-on, audit logs, a 2-hour SLA, a dedicated Slack channel and executive dashboards that feed Tableau, Power BI and Looker. An optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page actions, which suits large companies that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Enterprises short on people to act on the data, who want BI dashboards and audit logs.

Scrunch AI publishes one self-serve plan and sells everything else through a quote. Core costs $250 a month and includes 125 prompts, 5,000 responses a month, five user licences and Google single sign-on, which is enough for a pilot with a small team.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price and five users, with nine engines available on Enterprise.

Rankscale is the only tool here where the enterprise price is on the website. Enterprise is $780 a month for 12,000 credits, up to 48,000 answers, with REST API access and a dedicated partner. Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral are on every paid plan.

Best for: Teams that need a published enterprise price and the widest engine list.

Otterly.AI has the lowest entry price here, with unlimited team members on every plan and unlimited workspaces from the Standard plan, which helps when several business units want their own view. It is a lighter product than the five above, and SSO sits on its Enterprise plan, which starts from 1,000 prompts.

Best for: Business units that want their own workspace at a low price.

The most common mistake is buying for the pilot. A team runs a trial on one brand and one market, picks the tool with the friendliest entry price and finds out in month four that adding other markets, other teams and SSO moves them onto a quote that looks nothing like the trial.

Before you start a trial, write down three numbers: how many people will need to log in within a year, how many markets you sell in, and whether IT will require SSO. Then ask every vendor to price that.

Enterprise AI brand mention tracking is mostly a question of fit with how a large company buys. Peec AI is the strongest overall choice because users and markets do not drive its price, SSO can be enforced, and its source analysis shows what to fix instead of only how you rank.

Profound is the better route when a compliance review decides everything, AthenaHQ when you want BI dashboards and drafted work, Scrunch AI when you want a published entry price with five users, and Rankscale when you need a published enterprise price.

Whichever you pick, price your real workload, ask about SSO first and remember that the tool measures: what moves the number is being on the pages the engines read. The best AI brand mention tracking tools for enterprises are the ones that show you which pages those are.

What does an enterprise AI brand mention tracking tool cost?

Directionally, between $245 and $780 a month on published plans for 150 to 350 daily prompts: Peec AI Pro at $245 and Advanced at $495, Scrunch AI Core at $250 for 125 prompts, Otterly.AI Premium at $489 and Rankscale at $385 to $780. On Peec AI that is $1.41 to $1.63 per prompt with unlimited users. Once SSO is required, every tool here is a custom quote. The spread is driven by users and markets more than by features.

If more than a handful of people will log in, IT will usually ask for it. Every tool here puts SSO on Enterprise or a custom plan, so plan the budget for that contract instead of the self-serve tier.

How many prompts does an enterprise need?

A hundred to a hundred and fifty per brand and market. Start with the questions your sales team hears, then the comparisons buyers make between you and named competitors. More markets multiply the set. More product pages usually should not.

SEO usually owns the measurement. What breaks is the fix, because much of it means getting mentioned on sites you do not control, which sits with PR or communications. Agree that split before you buy.
